articles.title: Bringing Medication into Spain
articles.excerpt: The paperwork for an ordinary prescription, the separate permit required for ADHD stimulants and other controlled substances, and the one thing you must never do: mail a refill.
articles.content:
Spain doesn't stop Americans at the border over a bottle of blood-pressure pills, but it does have real rules — and one of them, for a short list of common medications, involves a permit you need to apply for before you fly. Get the basics right and this is a non-issue; get them wrong and you risk a medication seized at customs on a trip where you actually need it. Here's exactly what's required, split into the ordinary case and the controlled-substance case, because they're genuinely different procedures.

Ordinary prescription medication: the 3-month rule

For everyday prescriptions — blood pressure, cholesterol, thyroid, birth control, and the like — Spain allows travelers to bring a personal-use supply covering roughly up to three months of treatment. Keep every pill or liquid in its original pharmacy-labeled packaging, with the name on the label matching your passport. Carry either your original U.S. prescription or a signed letter from your doctor stating your name, the medical condition, and the dosage — ideally naming the generic (INN) drug, since U.S. brand names generally don't exist in Spain and a border officer or a Spanish pharmacist won't recognize them.

Why the generic name matters

A prescription that just says a U.S. brand name is far less useful in Spain than one that also lists the active ingredient. If you need to see a Spanish doctor for a refill mid-trip — which is your only option, since a Spanish pharmacy legally cannot fill a foreign prescription — the generic name is what lets them match it to the local equivalent quickly.

Controlled substances: ADHD stimulants, opioids, and benzodiazepines need a permit

If any of your medications are narcotics or psychotropics — ADHD stimulants like Adderall, Ritalin, or Concerta; opioid painkillers like Oxycodone, Tramadol, or codeine combinations; or anxiety medications like Xanax or Valium — the 3-month personal-use rule above does not simply apply on its own. These are internationally controlled substances, and Spain requires a formal traveler's authorization from AEMPS (the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices) before you can legally bring them across the border. You cannot just pack them and hope customs doesn't ask.

How to apply

Apply by email to AEMPS at least 10 days before departure (the current address is published on the AEMPS website under its traveler-medication section — addresses have appeared in slightly different forms across sources, so pull it directly from aemps.gob.es rather than copying one from memory). Attach PDF copies of: your passport, your flight itinerary, your original U.S. prescription, and a medical certificate from your doctor detailing your diagnosis, daily dosage, and the total quantity you're bringing — capped at roughly a 3-month supply, matching the general rule. Adderall in particular has no direct Spanish equivalent and draws extra scrutiny, so don't skip this step assuming a small quantity will go unnoticed.

What never to do: mailing a refill

Do not ship or mail medication — controlled or not — from the U.S. to a hotel or apartment in Barcelona. Spanish customs law prohibits individuals from receiving medication by international mail, and shipments that arrive this way are routinely confiscated and destroyed at the border, with no refund and no appeal that helps your trip. If you're going to run short, the fix is a Spanish doctor's visit for a new local prescription, not a package from home.

Practical packing checklist

  • Carry-on, not checked luggage. Keep all medication with you in case a checked bag is delayed or lost.
  • Original packaging always, even for a partial-use bottle — a loose pill organizer with no label is the fastest way to invite questions at customs.
  • Two copies of your prescription/letter — one in your bag, a photo saved to your phone.
  • Check quantity against the ~3-month cap if your trip runs long, and start the AEMPS process early for anything controlled — 10 days is a minimum, not a guarantee if the office is backed up.
  • No fixed customs value threshold exists for personal-use medicine — the standard is that the quantity plausibly matches a personal treatment course, not a specific euro amount, so a reasonable supply for your trip length is what protects you, not a number you calculate in advance.

The bottom line

For ordinary prescriptions, Spain is genuinely easy: original packaging, a prescription or doctor's letter, roughly three months' worth, done. It's only the controlled-substance list — stimulants, strong painkillers, certain anti-anxiety medications — where the extra AEMPS paperwork exists, and it exists precisely because these are the medications every country scrutinizes at its border. Handle that permit before you fly rather than at the airport, and never let a refill travel by mail, and this becomes a non-event in an otherwise smooth trip.

FAQ

How much prescription medication can I bring into Spain?

For ordinary, non-controlled prescriptions, roughly up to a 3-month personal-use supply, kept in original pharmacy-labeled packaging with your name matching your passport, plus your prescription or a doctor's letter.

Can I bring Adderall to Spain?

Only with a formal traveler's authorization from AEMPS applied for before departure — Adderall is a controlled stimulant with no direct Spanish equivalent. Email AEMPS at least 10 days ahead with your passport copy, itinerary, prescription, and a doctor's certificate detailing dosage and quantity.

Can a Spanish pharmacy refill my U.S. prescription?

No — Spanish pharmacies cannot fill a foreign prescription. If you run out, you'll need to see a Spanish doctor, who can issue a new local prescription; carrying your medication's generic (INN) name makes this much faster.

Can I have medication mailed to my hotel in Barcelona?

No. Spanish customs law prohibits individuals from receiving medication by international mail, and shipped medication is typically confiscated and destroyed at the border. Plan your supply before you leave instead.

Do I need to declare my medication at Spanish customs?

There's no fixed value threshold for personal-use medicine, so routine declaration usually isn't required for a reasonable supply — but carry your prescription or doctor's letter in case you're asked, and always get the AEMPS permit in advance for any controlled substance.

articles.title: Ferries from Barcelona to the Balearics: Fast vs Slow
articles.excerpt: Three operators, three islands, and a real choice between a fast daytime crossing and a cheaper overnight one — which one actually fits your trip.
articles.content:
Flying isn't the only way from Barcelona to Mallorca, Ibiza, or Menorca — a ferry gets you there too, and for some trips it's the better choice: no airport security theater, room to bring more luggage or a car, and if you take an overnight sailing, you save a hotel night while you sleep through the crossing. Here's how the crossing actually works, operator by operator and route by route.

Who runs the route

Three operators currently sail from Barcelona to the Balearics: Baleària and Trasmediterránea are the two long-established names, and GNV (Grandi Navi Veloci) also runs the corridor, with routes to Palma de Mallorca, Ibiza, and Mahón (Menorca) all appearing on its own schedule. All three depart from the Port de Barcelona, though not always from the same terminal — terminal assignment varies by operator and sometimes by sailing, so treat the terminal printed on your actual ticket as the source of truth rather than assuming. Give yourself extra time to find the right terminal, especially if you're bringing a car.

Fast ferry vs overnight ferry

Both formats run on this corridor, and the right one depends on what you're optimizing for. A fast ferry gets you there in a few hours during the day — it costs more, has fewer cabin options, and can feel rougher in bad weather, but it doesn't burn an evening. A conventional overnight ferry is cheaper, gives you a cabin to actually sleep in, and gets you off the boat rested with a full day ahead — the classic choice if you're bringing a car or traveling on a budget. Fast options aren't offered on every sailing or every route, so check what's actually running on your dates before assuming you have both choices.

Route by route

  • To Palma de Mallorca: a conventional crossing runs roughly 6–8.5 hours; where a fast option runs, expect roughly 2.5–3.5 hours.
  • To Ibiza: mostly overnight conventional sailings in the roughly 8–10 hour range; a same-day fast option isn't consistently available on this leg.
  • To Menorca (Mahón): more seasonal than the other two, running mostly in summer; where direct, figure roughly 7–10 hours conventional or 3.5–5.5 hours fast.

Fares move constantly with season and how far ahead you book, so check current pricing directly on the operator's site rather than trusting any number you see quoted elsewhere — this is exactly the kind of figure that goes stale within weeks.

Booking advice

In July and August, book weeks to months ahead, especially if you want a cabin or a car space — those sell out first. Foot passengers have more last-minute flexibility outside peak season. Compare the operator's own site (Baleària, Trasmediterránea, or GNV directly) against an aggregator like Direct Ferries — fares and terms aren't always mirrored, and the operator's own site is usually clearer about change and cancellation policies if your plans shift.

Getting to the terminal and what to expect on board

Check in at least an hour before departure for a foot-passenger ticket, and considerably more if you're bringing a car — vehicle check-in windows close earlier and queues build fast in summer. Foot passengers can typically bring normal luggage without the tight weight limits airlines enforce, which is one of the ferry's quiet advantages if you're arriving with beach gear, a car seat, or anything else awkward to fly with. On board, expect the basics — seating lounges, a café or bar, deck access — with overnight sailings adding cabins ranging from a shared berth to a private outside cabin with a window; book the cabin grade early in summer, since the cheapest options sell out first.

Frequency changes a lot by season

Summer (roughly June–September) brings daily or near-daily sailings on the Palma and Ibiza routes, with Menorca's schedule filling in alongside them. Outside that window, frequency drops — sometimes to a few sailings a week per route — so a winter or shoulder-season trip needs more schedule-checking up front than a summer one, where you can be more relaxed about locking in the exact day.

Which one should you pick

  • Traveling light and time-limited: the fast ferry, when your route and dates offer one.
  • Bringing a car, or watching your budget: the overnight conventional ferry — book a cabin and treat the crossing as a free night's accommodation.
  • Prone to seasickness: the larger conventional ferries generally handle rough water more comfortably than a fast catamaran-style vessel.
  • Traveling with family: the slower boat's extra space and onboard amenities tend to suit a family better than a fast, no-frills crossing.

Whichever you choose, the ferry is a genuinely pleasant alternative to flying for this route — no shrinking security lines, no baggage fees that creep up with every airline, and on the overnight option, a crossing that quietly does double duty as your hotel for the night.

FAQ

Which ferry companies sail from Barcelona to the Balearics?

Baleària, Trasmediterránea, and GNV (Grandi Navi Veloci) all currently operate this corridor, sailing to Palma de Mallorca, Ibiza, and Mahón (Menorca).

How long is the ferry from Barcelona to Mallorca?

A conventional crossing runs roughly 6–8.5 hours; a fast ferry, where available, takes roughly 2.5–3.5 hours. Exact schedules change by season, so check the operator's current timetable.

Is it better to take a fast ferry or an overnight ferry to the Balearics?

Depends on your priorities: fast saves a travel day but costs more and offers less comfort in rough seas; overnight is cheaper, gives you a cabin to sleep in, and works well if you're bringing a car or traveling on a budget.

Can I take a car on the ferry to Mallorca or Ibiza?

Yes, all three operators carry vehicles, but car spaces sell out weeks ahead in summer — book well in advance if you want to bring one.

How far ahead should I book a Balearic ferry?

For July–August sailings, book weeks to months ahead, especially for a cabin or car space. Outside peak season, foot passengers have more last-minute flexibility.

articles.title: When a Balearic Ferry Cancels, and What You're Owed
articles.excerpt: Weather cancels Balearic ferries more often than flights get cancelled — here's what EU law actually guarantees you, and what to do the moment it happens.
articles.content:
A ferry to the Balearics is a genuinely pleasant way to travel — right up until a stretch of wind cancels your sailing and you're standing in a terminal with no clear idea what happens next. It's a real enough risk that it's worth knowing your rights before you're the one asking. Here's what actually causes a cancellation, what EU law entitles you to, and what to actually do in the moment.

Why these ferries get cancelled

The overwhelming cause is weather — specifically wind and sea state (wave height) exceeding what's safe for the vessel type, which happens on this corridor more than travelers expect, especially in the shoulder and winter months but genuinely possible any time. Operational or technical issues happen too, but far less often than a straightforward call that the crossing isn't safe that day.

Your rights under EU law

Ferries in the EU — including this route — fall under EU Regulation (EC) No 1177/2010 on the rights of passengers traveling by sea. In broad terms: if your sailing is cancelled, or delayed past a set threshold at departure, you're entitled to a choice between a full refund or free re-routing under comparable conditions to your original booking. While you wait, the operator has care obligations — meals and refreshments, and accommodation if the delay runs overnight. Cash compensation for a late arrival is more limited and narrower in practice, and generally does not apply when the cause is “extraordinary circumstances” — which weather typically counts as. Don't expect a cash payout for a storm cancellation; expect a refund or a re-route, and the operator covering you while you wait.

What operators actually do

In practice, operators generally offer a spot on the next available sailing — often the next day once conditions clear — or a full refund, and this can usually be arranged online or at the port ticket office. Practices vary by operator and by how severe the disruption is, so contact the carrier as soon as you know your sailing is affected, and keep every piece of documentation: your original ticket, any confirmation of rebooking, and receipts for anything the airline or ferry line didn't cover directly.

Does travel insurance help

Sometimes, and it's worth having regardless. A standard policy's trip interruption or transport disruption coverage is what would reimburse costs the ferry line itself doesn't — a missed onward connection, an extra hotel night while you wait for the next sailing — but plain trip-cancellation coverage usually doesn't extend to this. Weather-caused disruptions tend to be covered more often than operator-caused ones like insolvency, but the exact wording varies policy to policy, so check what you actually bought before you need it rather than after.

Spotting it coming, before you're at the terminal

Weather-driven cancellations aren't usually a total surprise — a forecast showing strong wind or a big swell in the 24 hours before your sailing is a real warning sign. Check the operator's own status page or app the morning of travel rather than relying on a general weather app; the ferry line knows its own vessel's operating limits, and its status page updates faster than a news report will. If a cancellation looks likely, it's worth having a backup plan already in mind — a later sailing that day, or knowing that Baleària, Trasmediterránea, and GNV don't all necessarily cancel the same departure at the same time, so a competing operator's later sailing can sometimes be the fastest way across if your own is scrapped.

What to do the moment it happens

  • Go straight to the operator's desk or app — don't wait in a general information line if the ferry company has its own counter.
  • Ask explicitly for your options: next available sailing, or a refund — both are your right, and it's the operator's job to offer them, not yours to negotiate for them.
  • Keep every receipt for meals or a hotel the operator doesn't directly cover, in case you need to claim them back.
  • Don't assume cash compensation is coming for a weather cancellation — plan your next move around a refund or re-route, not a payout.
  • If you have an onward connection at risk (a flight, a hotel booking on the island), start adjusting it as soon as the cancellation is confirmed rather than waiting to see if the next sailing works out.

The bottom line

A cancelled Balearic ferry isn't rare, and it isn't a disaster either, as long as you know what you're entitled to going in: a refund or a free re-route, meals and lodging while you wait if it runs overnight, and an operator that's legally on the hook for making that happen. Bring travel insurance for the costs that fall outside the ferry line's obligations, keep your paperwork, and treat a weather cancellation as an inconvenience to manage rather than a fight to have.

FAQ

What happens if my Balearic ferry gets cancelled?

Under EU Regulation 1177/2010, you're entitled to a choice of a full refund or free re-routing on comparable terms, plus meals/refreshments and accommodation from the operator if the delay runs overnight.

Do I get cash compensation for a cancelled ferry?

Usually not for weather-related cancellations — these typically count as “extraordinary circumstances,” which are generally excluded from cash compensation under the regulation. Expect a refund or re-route instead.

Why do ferries to the Balearics get cancelled so often?

Mostly wind and sea state exceeding safe operating limits for the vessel — more common in shoulder and winter months, though possible any time of year. Mechanical or operational issues happen too, but less often.

Does travel insurance cover a cancelled ferry?

Often partially — a policy's trip-interruption or transport-disruption coverage can reimburse costs like a missed onward connection or an extra hotel night, though plain cancellation coverage usually doesn't apply. Check your specific policy wording.

What should I do first if my ferry is cancelled?

Go directly to the operator's desk or app and ask for your options — the next available sailing or a refund. Keep every receipt for anything you pay out of pocket while you wait.

articles.title: What to Expect When a Spanish Hospital Bills You
articles.excerpt: You will be treated first and billed after — but public and private care follow different rules, and only one document trail gets you reimbursed back home.
articles.content:
Getting sick or hurt on a trip is stressful enough without wondering how the bill works — and Spain's hospital system, generous as it is with its own residents, treats an American tourist differently in one specific way: you will absolutely be treated, but you will also, eventually, be billed. Here's exactly how that plays out, in both the public and private systems, and what paperwork actually gets you reimbursed once you're home.

The public ER: treated first, billed after

Spain's public hospital emergency departments (urgencias) triage and treat anyone who walks in, regardless of nationality or ability to pay — no insurance card is demanded at the door, and true emergency stabilization cannot legally be refused. Where it changes for a U.S. tourist is afterward: once your care is no longer classified as immediate emergency stabilization, you're billed, since you're not covered the way an EU resident is under Spain's public system. The invoice may be handed to you at discharge or mailed to you afterward, depending on the hospital, and one reported wrinkle worth knowing is that some facilities route billing through third-party intermediaries that can inflate the final amount — not universal, but worth double-checking any invoice that looks unusually high.

Private clinics: pay first, claim later

A private clinic or hospital works the opposite way around: expect to provide a card guarantee or upfront payment before non-emergency treatment, especially anything beyond a basic consultation. In exchange, private facilities are generally faster, more likely to have English-speaking staff, and issue a clean itemized invoice designed for you to submit straight to your travel insurer — which is exactly the point of paying upfront rather than waiting on a mailed bill.

Roughly what things cost

Treat these only as a rough, unverified sense of scale, not fixed prices — check current rates and never plan your trip around a number you read online: a private walk-in consultation runs roughly in the tens to low hundreds of euros; a public ER visit for a non-EU tourist, before any tests or imaging, is often in a similar range and up from there; an overnight stay runs materially more, and an ambulance ride is typically billed separately from the hospital visit itself.

What to keep for reimbursement

  • The itemized invoice (factura / factura desglosada) — a summary total isn't enough for most U.S. insurers.
  • The medical report (informe médico) — diagnosis and treatment in writing.
  • A discharge summary, if you were admitted.
  • Any prescriptions issued during treatment.
  • Every payment receipt — the hospital's, the pharmacy's, the ambulance's, all of it.

Ask for English or bilingual copies before you leave the facility if at all possible — chasing paperwork by mail from Barcelona after you've flown home is far harder than requesting it in person.

The right first stop, not just the ER

Not everything that feels alarming abroad needs a hospital. For anything short of a genuine emergency, a pharmacist can often assess and treat you directly, and a private walk-in clinic is usually faster and cheaper than the public ER for something that needs a doctor but isn't life-threatening — a bad ear infection, a sprained ankle, a stomach bug that won't quit. Save the public ER, or calling 112, for chest pain, difficulty breathing, major trauma, or anything that genuinely can't wait — both the wait time and the eventual bill tend to scale with how the system classifies your visit, so matching the venue to the actual severity of the problem saves you money as well as time.

Why travel insurance isn't optional here

U.S. Medicare and Medicaid do not cover care outside the United States, and most standard U.S. health plans stop at the border too. Without travel insurance, you're paying the full bill out of pocket in the moment, with reimbursement — if any — coming later and only with the paperwork above. A travel medical policy with reasonable coverage limits turns a potentially serious financial hit into a manageable claim, and it's genuinely one of the highest-value purchases you can make for a trip to Spain.

The bottom line

Nobody in Spain will turn you away from emergency care over money, but nobody's going to quietly absorb the cost either — public hospitals bill afterward, private ones bill upfront, and either way, the invoice eventually lands on you unless insurance is standing behind you. Carry a policy before you need one, ask for every piece of documentation on the way out the door, and treat the paperwork with the same seriousness as the visit itself.

FAQ

Will a Spanish hospital treat me without insurance?

Yes — public emergency departments treat anyone regardless of nationality or ability to pay, and cannot legally refuse true emergency stabilization. You will, however, be billed afterward for care beyond that immediate stabilization.

Do I pay upfront at a Spanish hospital?

At a private clinic or hospital, generally yes — expect a card guarantee or upfront payment before non-emergency treatment. Public hospitals more often bill afterward, at discharge or by mail.

What documents do I need for a travel insurance claim after treatment in Spain?

The itemized invoice (factura), the medical report (informe médico), a discharge summary if admitted, any prescriptions issued, and every payment receipt — ideally in English or bilingual copies requested before you leave the facility.

Does Medicare cover me in Spain?

No — Medicare and Medicaid do not cover care outside the United States, and most standard U.S. health plans don't either. Travel medical insurance is the practical substitute for this trip.

How much does an ER visit cost in Barcelona for a tourist?

Costs vary and change over time, so treat any figure as a rough approximation rather than a fixed price — a basic visit is typically in the tens to low hundreds of euros before tests or imaging, with an overnight stay running materially more. Confirm current costs and don't plan around an old number.

articles.title: What Closes on a Spanish Public Holiday
articles.excerpt: National, Catalan, and Barcelona's own local holidays each close different things — and one popular festival everyone assumes is a day off actually isn't.
articles.content:
Barcelona stacks three layers of public holidays on top of each other — national Spanish holidays, Catalonia's own regional days, and two local holidays the city council picks itself — and each one closes a slightly different slice of the city. Land on the wrong day without checking, and you'll find banks shuttered and your favorite neighborhood restaurant dark; land on the right day and you'll catch a genuine local celebration. Here's the full picture, including one very popular date that surprises people by NOT being a day off.

Spain's national holidays

Ten fixed national holidays apply everywhere in Spain: New Year's Day (Jan 1), Epiphany (Jan 6), Labour Day (May 1), the Assumption (Aug 15), National Day (Oct 12), All Saints' Day (Nov 1), Constitution Day (Dec 6), the Immaculate Conception (Dec 8), and Christmas (Dec 25) — plus Good Friday, which is fixed by the Church calendar rather than a set date each year. Confirm the exact dates for your travel year against the official calendar rather than assuming they never move; several genuinely do shift slightly, and when one lands on a weekend, businesses don't always get a substitute day off.

Catalonia's own regional holidays

On top of the national list, Catalonia observes its own regional days: Easter Monday (a genuine day off here, unlike most of Spain), Sant Joan / St John's Day (June 24), the Diada Nacional de Catalunya (September 11), and Sant Esteve / Boxing Day (December 26).

The Sant Jordi myth

Here's the surprise: Sant Jordi (April 23) — the beloved book-and-rose festival that fills La Rambla with stalls every spring — is not an official public holiday. Shops, offices, and restaurants stay open as normal; it's a major civic and cultural celebration, not a day off. If you're planning around it expecting empty streets and closed businesses, plan again — it's actually one of the busiest, most normal-hours days on the calendar, just wrapped in flowers and paperbacks.

Barcelona's own two local holidays

Beyond the national and regional layers, Barcelona's city council designates two of its own local holidays each year — and unlike the others, these can genuinely change from year to year by council decree, so treat any specific date as tied to the current calendar year rather than a fixed tradition. For 2026, the two are Whit Monday / Pentecost Monday (May 25) and La Mercè (September 24), the city's own patron-saint festival and its biggest annual celebration. Check the current year's designation before building a trip around either date, since the first of the two is not guaranteed to repeat.

What actually closes vs. stays open

  • Closed: most independent shops, banks, government offices, and post offices.
  • Mostly open, sometimes reduced hours: malls, large chains, and shops in the designated tourist zones.
  • Mixed: restaurants — neighborhood, non-tourist spots often close, while tourist-area restaurants, bars, and cafés mostly stay open.
  • Usually still running: museums, though many switch to a Sunday-style or special holiday schedule rather than closing outright — check the specific venue.
  • Reduced service: public transport runs its Sunday/holiday timetable (horario festivo) — less frequent, still running.
  • Always available: pharmacies, via the rotating duty (farmacia de guardia) system.

Watch for the “puente” effect

Spain has a habit that amplifies all of this: when a holiday falls on a Tuesday or Thursday, many locals take the connecting Monday or Friday off too, turning a single day off into a four-day puente (literally, “bridge”). It isn't an official extra holiday — offices and many shops still technically could open — but in practice, a lot of Barcelona quietly empties out for the long weekend anyway, especially outside the tourist core. If your dates land right around a Tuesday or Thursday holiday, expect a noticeably quieter, more closed-up city than the official calendar alone would suggest, and book any restaurant you care about accordingly.

Planning around the calendar

Book restaurant reservations further ahead around any of these dates, and check individual museum or attraction hours for the exact day rather than assuming normal service — this is doubly true for booking timed-entry tickets for anything popular, since holiday crowding compounds the usual advance-booking pressure at Barcelona's major sights. If your dates land near mid-August, note that many small, family-run businesses close for their own vacation around the Assumption holiday regardless of the official calendar — a separate pattern worth planning around on its own.

The bottom line

Three layers — national, Catalan, and Barcelona's own — each close a different slice of the city, and the one date everyone assumes is a holiday, Sant Jordi, actually isn't one at all. Check the current year's specific dates before you travel, especially for Barcelona's two local days, which the council resets annually, and you'll never be caught out by a shuttered bank or a fully-booked restaurant on a day you didn't see coming.

FAQ

Is Sant Jordi a public holiday in Barcelona?

No — despite being one of Catalonia's most beloved celebrations, Sant Jordi (April 23) is a cultural festival, not an official public holiday. Shops, offices, and restaurants stay open as normal.

What are Barcelona's local holidays?

The city council designates two local holidays each year, which can change annually. For 2026, they are Whit Monday / Pentecost Monday (May 25) and La Mercè (September 24), the city's own patron-saint festival.

Do banks close on Spanish public holidays?

Yes — banks, government offices, and post offices close on national, regional, and local holidays alike, along with most independent shops.

Are restaurants open on public holidays in Barcelona?

It depends on the neighborhood — non-tourist, residential-area restaurants often close, while restaurants, bars, and cafés in tourist zones mostly stay open.

Is Easter Monday a holiday in Barcelona?

Yes — Easter Monday is a genuine regional public holiday in Catalonia, unlike in most of the rest of Spain, where it isn't observed.
